doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: College before college: teenage awareness of the greats
summary: Schoenberg says as a teen he thought mentors like Hinton were normal life; Rowe shares his own Mangione experience.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You went to college before you went to college.
Yes. You know that’s a good —
That’s the way I feel about it. Because you can’t pay for that stuff that you got.

Absolutely. A question you asked a while ago was like did I realize or did I know like you mentioned you were in a car with Milt Hinton over here asleep on your shoulder. You’re saying now wait a minute, this is not just some old bass player, this is Milton J. Hinton and this is Fiddler Claude Williams or these people. And the only way to answer your question is you know you were older when that happened to you, I assume you were in your 30s or something.

For me in my teens frankly I thought that’s the way the life was. And I mean I treated them with great respect. Of course I think now about how I behaved and I go oh my God. But no I mean I had no idea of how great it was.
Yeah. In some ways it’s great. I mean when I was in my teens I had a couple of experiences but they were a different level, like Chuck and Gap Mangione in Rochester.

Okay? So that was my thing. And at the time it was the same. I was respectful, I was a little envious, they’re doing what I would like to do. But and then later on when you know the history of these people. So that’s a heck of a story. Jazz has been called America’s only original art form.
